column1: In a GBC (Great Ball Contraption), what is the fundamental architectural invariant that enables modules designed by different builders to interoperate?
column2: A standardized handoff protocol—consistent positional standards, timing contracts, and mechanical clearances at input/output interfaces—so any module can receive from and deliver to its neighbors reliably.

column1: What target throughput range (balls per minute) should a well-designed GBC pathway sustain?
column2: Between 60 and 180 balls per minute (roughly 1 to 3 balls per second per pathway).

column1: Why must every lift mechanism in a GBC restore gravitational potential energy to circulating balls?
column2: Because inelastic collisions between balls and structural elements (coefficient of restitution ~0.4-0.6) dissipate kinetic energy, so lifts must re-add potential energy to sustain continuous circulation.

column1: State the gear ratio formula used in GBC drivetrain design and what a 40-tooth gear driven by an 8-tooth pinion yields.
column2: R = N_driven / N_driver. A 40-tooth driven gear with an 8-tooth driver pinion gives a 5:1 reduction, multiplying torque by 5 and dividing speed by 5.

column1: What is the approximate per-stage efficiency loss in a Lego gear mesh, and what does this mean for a 4-stage compound gear train?
column2: Each mesh loses ~2-5% of input power to friction and deflection; a 4-stage compound train therefore loses roughly 8-18% of input power before reaching the output shaft.

column1: What is the recommended motor load 'sweet spot' (as a percentage of stall torque) for reliable long-duration GBC operation?
column2: Between 30% and 70% of stall torque—enough authority to handle ball impacts while avoiding thermal stress during 8-12 hour display runs.

column1: Approximately what stall torque do the Lego M-motor and XL-motor produce at 9V, and why does this matter for module design?
column2: M-motor: ~0.04 Nm stall torque. XL-motor: ~0.4 Nm stall torque (10x more). This tenfold difference fundamentally changes which mechanical architectures (lifting vs. light conveying) are viable for a given motor choice.

column1: What is the 'inheritance' invariant of ball velocity between cascading GBC modules?
column2: Ball velocity is not independently set by each module—the exit speed from one module's output becomes the entry condition for the next module's intake, forming a coupled energy contract across the chain.

column1: Why is a curved receiver channel preferred over a flat horizontal tile for catching a dropped ball in a GBC module?
column2: A flat tile causes chaotic, unpredictable bouncing, while a curved channel converts most of the vertical velocity component into controlled, predictable horizontal momentum through deflection.

column1: What is 'lane geometry determinism' and what minimum physical feature enforces it at a bifurcation point?
column2: It requires that a ball's path-separation decision be mechanically unambiguous (no straddling). A reliable passive divider needs a ridge narrower than the ball diameter—minimum 1-stud-wide (8mm), chamfered or studless—contacted while the ball still carries 60-70% of entry momentum.

column1: What is 'conservation of ball flux' in a closed-loop GBC system, and what happens when it's violated?
column2: In steady state, every module's throughput must converge to the same global equilibrium rate since no balls enter or leave the loop. If upstream delivery exceeds downstream processing capacity, balls accumulate at the interface buffer, leading to mechanical interference, motor stall, or spillage.

column1: Why does 'timing coherence' degrade over time between two asynchronous GBC modules, and what are the two mitigation strategies?
column2: Because modules run on independent motors with no shared electrical clock, small cycle-time differences accumulate as phase drift, eventually causing simultaneous deliveries that overwhelm buffers. Mitigations: (1) generous physical buffering to tolerate stochastic variation, or (2) mechanical feedback coupling to impose soft synchronization.
